title: Xi addresses China and the world in rare public speech on AI
gist: At the World AI Conference, Xi Jinping delivered a rare public AI speech centred on humans collaborating with machine intelligence and, for the first time publicly, named AI-specific 'loss of control' (失控) risk — though MERICS argues the CCP's notion of control means preserving human judgment and authority rather than the alignment and superintelligence risks that dominate Western safety debates, with possible restrictions on Chinese open-source models looming.

themes.theme: Xi's WAIC speech as a first-order AI policy signal

insights.claim: Xi Jinping used his in-person debut at the World AI Conference to deliver one of his most significant public interventions on AI to date, whereas his richest previous AI remarks came from Politburo Study Sessions that outsiders saw only as summaries.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese AI policy signalling has moved from internal party channels to public forums — the speech text is now tradeable information.
insights.locator: Xi Jinping chose his in-person debut

insights.claim: The Chinese leadership's AI vision, matured over a decade, centres on humans collaborating with machine intelligence, using recurring concepts of integration, connectivity and collaboration that reflect CCP expectations that physical AI will boost growth, development and societal wellbeing.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Beijing frames AI as a growth and productivity input, implying continued state support for deployment rather than restraint.
insights.quote: How to get along with thinking machines?
insights.locator: What emerges starkly from his speech

insights.claim: Agents and embodied AI were in the spotlight at this year's World AI Conference, consistent with the leadership's emphasis on physical AI.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese robotics and agent stacks sit where policy attention and capital are converging.
insights.locator: Not surprisingly, agents and embodied AI

insights.claim: 'Controllability' (可控) has been a consistent leitmotif in Chinese AI policy, but the term's meaning varies widely and can refer to political control, cybersecurity, or a preference for domestic technology.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Do not read Chinese 'AI control' language as Western-style safety commitment — parse which sense is meant before drawing regulatory conclusions.
insights.quote: “Controllability” (可控) has been a consistent leitmotif in Chinese AI policy
insights.locator: A precondition for all this, in the CCP’s view

insights.claim: Xi Jinping made his first known public reference to AI-specific 'loss of control' (失控) risk, having previously raised the alarm only about future technologies in general at a January Politburo Study Session.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A top-level rhetorical shift that could precede binding Chinese AI safety rules — a new compliance vector for AI developers in China.
insights.locator: What is new and more interesting

insights.claim: It is not clear from Xi's speech or other policy signals that China's leaders are worried about alignment risks as the international AI safety community understands them, though his distinction between 'inherent and secondary risks' (内生和衍生风险) hints at concern about safety flaws in model design.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese and Western AI risk agendas may be verbally convergent but substantively different — discount hopes of quick international safety alignment.
insights.locator: Still, it is not immediately clear

insights.claim: An essay in the party's top theory journal published a day before Xi's speech suggests the CCP is leaning toward a broad definition of human control that preserves human judgment, subjectivity and power in the AI age, in contrast to Western safety debates focused on existential risk from superintelligence.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: China's AI governance is likely to produce human-authority rules rather than capability limits — different compliance burdens than Western frameworks.
insights.locator: If we take an essay that appeared in the party’s top theory journal

themes.theme: Possible export controls on Chinese open-source models

insights.claim: Media reports suggest restrictions on access to Chinese open-source AI models could be on the horizon, though it is unclear whether the emerging AI export-control discussion stems from genuine alignment concerns or from Beijing's growing worry about technology and know-how leakage.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Global availability of Chinese open-weight models is a policy variable now — anyone building on them carries supply risk.
insights.locator: Restrictions on access to Chinese open-source models could be on the horizon

insights.claim: The decisive test is whether top-level signals such as Xi's speech translate into accelerated technical AI safety research in China or into a tighter regulatory grip on the AI industry.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A clean binary to monitor: safety-lab funding announcements versus new licensing rules will tell you which way Chinese AI policy is turning.
insights.quote: It will be key to watch whether top-level signals like Xi’s speech result in an acceleration of technical safety research—or a tighter regulatory grip on the industry.
insights.locator: It will be key to watch
